source: Metacognitive Monitoring Battery (2026) cross-domain benchmark for LLM self-monitoring
finding: Twenty frontier models were probed with KEEP/WITHDRAW and BET/decline after each forced-choice answer, built on Nelson-Narens and Koriat-Goldsmith. Accuracy rank and monitoring rank were roughly inverted.
numbers: 20 models, 524 items, 6 domains. GLM-5 ranked 1st on accuracy but 9th on monitoring sensitivity. Claude Haiku 4.5 ranked 13th on accuracy, 2nd on monitoring. Sonnet 4.6 ranked 1st on monitoring (mean withdraw delta +39.4%) but 9th on accuracy.
limits: Behavioural probe may measure response style as well as monitoring; n=20 models; convergent validity not shown.
agent_relevance: Do not pick the model that monitors by its accuracy rank. A strong solver can be a weak monitor, so S6 monitoring should be measured per model, or done by code.

source: Metacognitive Monitoring Battery (2026) blanket confidence
finding: Most models answered KEEP and BET on nearly everything, including adversarial items they got wrong. Accuracy-only benchmarks hide this.
numbers: On the six adversarial foils of task T1, 17 of 20 models scored 0% while answering KEEP+BET on every item. Profile A models kept more than 95% of answers whether right or wrong.
limits: Six foil items only; the foils are designed traps.
agent_relevance: A model's own keep/withdraw choice carries little signal on hard traps. Supports G10 and code-side checks instead of self-report.

source: Metacognitive Monitoring Battery (2026) retrospective versus prospective dissociation
finding: Monitoring (after answering) and regulation (asking for help or answering directly before answering) were only weakly linked across models. Some models monitor without regulating.
numbers: Pearson r = .17 (95% CI -.29 to +.57), n = 20 models; power for r=.5 only .62. Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 had strong withdraw delta but answered directly 98.6% of the time on T6. Gemma 27B regulated without monitoring. Haiku 4.5 did both.
limits: Underpowered; the authors say the correlation alone does not prove independence. Dissociation rests on exemplar models.
agent_relevance: Supports the Nelson-Narens split: a monitoring signal does not by itself produce control. This is the gap our code-side controller fills.

source: Metacognitive Monitoring Battery (2026) scale and architecture effects
finding: No single scaling law for monitoring. Three model families showed three different trends with size.
numbers: T2 withdraw delta: Qwen 80B +30.1%, 235B +21.8%, Coder 480B +11.2% (falls with scale). GPT-5.4 nano +17.1%, mini +22.4%, 5.4 +27.7% (rises). Gemma 1B +18.3%, 12B +18.3%, 27B +16.7% (flat).
limits: Items and post-training differ across families; the authors cannot separate training from architecture.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a bigger model monitors better. Re-measure monitoring when the model is swapped.

source: Metacognitive Monitoring Battery (2026) reasoning model anomaly
finding: DeepSeek R1 withdrew almost everything, which looks like blanket withdrawal rather than selective monitoring.
numbers: R1 declined 98.6% of T6 items and kept at most about 10% of answers, correct or not, while its scored accuracy was 100% on T1, T3, T4, T5. A non-reasoning sibling (V3.2) kept 97.8% on T2.
limits: One model; the authors treat it as behavioural withdrawal and exclude it from rankings.
agent_relevance: Long reasoning can surface doubt but not make it selective. Doubt must be gated by a code check (G1).

source: Cao et al. (2026) LLMs know when they know, but do not act on it: a metacognitive harness for test-time scaling
finding: A Nelson-Narens style harness separates monitoring from reasoning: a pre-solve FOK and post-solve JOL feed a small calibrated controller that decides trust, retry, stop or aggregate. It raised a fixed Claude Sonnet 4.6.
numbers: Pooled 1,859 examples: pass@1 48.3 to 56.9 (+8.6). HLE-Verified 48.0 to 60.0. LiveCodeBench v6 74.3 to 84.3. R-Bench-V 36.1 to 41.1. LiveCodeBench Hard split +19.6.
limits: One base model; budgets matched only when possible; per-benchmark N and intervals not extracted here; code not released at time of paper.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of our S6 idea (monitor up, control down). The control was learned code over self-reported scores, not model choice.

source: Cao et al. (2026) metacognitive harness: model does not use its own confidence
finding: Without the harness, models report confidence that predicts correctness but do not spend more reasoning on low-confidence items.
numbers: Figure 1 of the paper: FOK and JOL separate correct from incorrect, yet normalised reasoning length does not rise for low-confidence items. Under the harness, mean attempts fall monotonically from low to high confidence.
limits: Shown in a figure; exact slopes not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Monitoring-to-control link is missing by default in LLMs. It has to be built outside the model.

source: Cao et al. (2026) metacognitive harness: where the gain sits
finding: Gain came from problems the model first doubted. High-confidence problems got no gain and a slight loss.
numbers: Accuracy by first-attempt JOL group, pass@1 to harness: low 0.16 to 0.42; medium 0.36 to 0.55; high 0.67 to 0.64.
limits: Groups defined by the same JOL the harness uses, so selection effects are possible.
agent_relevance: Fits G1 and G12: doubt only on a signal, and spend on the uncertain items. Over-checking confident items can cost a little.

source: Cao et al. (2026) metacognitive harness: confidence works across problems, not within
finding: Self-rated confidence tells which problem deserves more compute but not which attempt at that problem is best.
numbers: Median within-problem SD of JOL across attempts = 0.048; SD across problems = 0.270 (about 5.6 times wider). Max-JOL and last-answer aggregation were worse than a forced aggregator that sees traces but not scores.
limits: One model family and three benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Use confidence for the retry or stop decision only. Select among attempts with code checks, not self-confidence (G5).

source: Cao et al. (2026) metacognitive harness: ablations
finding: Every part helped: removing FOK or JOL hurt; a hand-made confidence rule was worse than the calibrated SVM; random retry and fixed-K retry were worse at comparable budget; full prior traces anchored later attempts to old mistakes.
numbers: Direction of each ablation reported in text; numeric deltas are in appendix tables, not recorded here. Of nine models, only Sonnet 4.6 passed every diagnosis row; Gemini 3 Flash was discriminative but miscalibrated; Gemma 4 had weak signal.
limits: Method may not transfer to weaker monitors.
agent_relevance: Retry should carry compact feedback, not full traces. A calibration step is needed before raw confidence is used as a control signal.

source: Oh and Gobet (2025) Monitor-Generate-Verify: formalising metacognitive theory for LM reasoning
finding: A conceptual architecture that maps Flavell and Nelson-Narens onto reasoning models, with a monitor step before generation. It offers no experiments of its own.
numbers: The paper states it offers no empirical validation. It cites a prefix dominance trap with nearly 20% accuracy loss when models commit early (from other work).
limits: NeurIPS 2025 workshop paper; the 20% figure is cited, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Treat as vocabulary only. Not evidence that a pre-generation monitor helps.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Large models are well calibrated on multiple-choice formats and can estimate P(True) for their own samples and P(IK) (I know) before answering. P(IK) is context sensitive.
numbers: P(True) improves with model size; samples with P(True) > 0.5 are far more often correct. 52B P(IK) rose from 18% to 78% when relevant source text was added. P(IK) calibration is poor on new task types.
limits: Anthropic-internal models up to 52B; format matters; calibration breaks out of distribution; RLHF models were miscalibrated until temperature was tuned.
agent_relevance: Supports a pre-solve FOK signal (S0 gate) but only after calibration on our own task class.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? Empirical evaluation of confidence elicitation
finding: Verbalised confidence is overconfident and weak at telling right from wrong. Agreement across several samples is much better than asking the model.
numbers: Vanilla verbalised confidence, GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% (50% is chance) across eight tasks. About 22.2% AUROC improvement from GPT-3 to GPT-4. GSM8K AUROC 54.8% with verbalised confidence versus 92.7% with 5 samples plus consistency. White-box gap: 0.522 versus 0.605 AUROC.
limits: Weak on professional-knowledge tasks; no method won everywhere; sample agreement is not independent evidence (G4).
agent_relevance: Code-computed agreement beats self-reported confidence as a monitoring signal. Matches our rule that code monitors, model acts.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Monitoring plus control inside the model, with no outside signal, did not help and often hurt. Earlier gains came from using the true answer label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 pass@1 GSM8K 75.9, CommonSenseQA 75.8, HotpotQA 26.0; after two self-correction rounds 74.7, 41.8, 25.0. GPT-4: 95.5, 82.0, 49.0 to 89.0, 80.0, 43.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5 to 88.0 (round 1) and 90.0 (round 2). Oracle-label correction: GPT-3.5 up to 84.3, 89.7, 29.0; GPT-4 up to 97.5, 85.5, 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% on GSM8K; when it changed, correct-to-wrong exceeded wrong-to-correct.
limits: Intrinsic setting only; external feedback (tools, tests) not covered. Oracle rows were read from a garbled text table layout.
agent_relevance: The monitor must be external (G2, G3). A model-only monitor is a failed meta level.

source: Metcalfe and Kornell (2005) A Region of Proximal Learning model of study time allocation
finding: Control follows monitoring in two parts: choose items by JOL (skip items judged known, then easiest unlearned first), and stop when the judged rate of learning nears zero. Eight experiments supported it.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=24): 20 of 24 said they chose items they did not know; chosen items were harder by norms (180.90 vs 138.64, t(23)=7.88, ES .73), true for 22 of 24. Exp 7: gamma between study time and JOL was -.34 for short-time and -.50 for long-time participants; the stopping rule differs by person.
limits: University students and paired associates; the authors note null study-time effects in earlier work (Mazzoni and Cornoldi, 1993) and that overall gamma hides the curve.
agent_relevance: Rival to the discrepancy-reduction rule: spend where learning is still moving, not just where the gap is biggest. Useful for the budget stop in S5/S6.

source: Thiede, Anderson and Therriault (2003) Accuracy of metacognitive monitoring affects learning of texts
finding: Better monitoring caused better regulation of restudy and better final scores. Accuracy was raised by writing keywords after a delay.
numbers: N=66 (df 2,63); three groups. Monitoring accuracy differed by group, F(2,63)=4.07. Regulation gamma: delayed-keyword .79 (SEM .11), immediate .35 (.17), no-keyword .36 (.15). Second-test old items .69 vs .53 vs .56. Texts selected for restudy: first test .27 vs .43/.44, second test .71 vs .51/.57. Number restudied did not differ.
limits: Monitoring accuracy was manipulated, so the causal chain is supported in this design; one university sample, expository texts. A later paper (search snippet only) notes a delay-versus-task-lag confound.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that the quality of the monitoring signal, not the amount of control, drives gains. Spend effort on the signal.

source: Rhodes and Tauber (2011) The influence of delaying judgments of learning on metacognitive accuracy: a meta-analytic review
finding: Delaying the JOL makes monitoring far more accurate. The delayed JOL effect is robust and has a small benefit on memory itself.
numbers: Meta-analysis 1: 4,554 participants, 112 effect sizes, g = 0.93 for relative accuracy (gamma). Meta-analysis 2: 3,807 participants, 98 effect sizes, g = 0.08 for memory.
limits: Abstract only (via OpenAlex); full paper not read. Theories (retrieval opportunity, cue match, diagnostic information) are not fully separated.
agent_relevance: A delayed, retrieval-based check is a better monitor than an immediate one. For the agent: grade an answer after a fresh, independent re-derivation, not right after writing it.

source: Finn (2008) Framing effects on metacognitive monitoring and control
finding: Telling people to remember or to forget the same items changed their JOLs and restudy choices, but not their recall. Control followed the judgment, not performance.
numbers: Exp 2 (N=46): recall .37 vs .40 (n.s.); JOL .56 vs .46; restudy choice .45 (remember) vs .65 (forget), t(44)=2.22. Exp 3 (N=42): restudy .36 vs .52. Exp 1A (N=48) JOL .51 vs .37. Delayed JOL (Exp 1B, N=40): gamma .91 and .75, framing effect gone. JOL-choice gammas about -.5 to -.76.
limits: Choices were not correlated with recall directly; framing could also change effort or demand. Page read through a summarising tool, not a PDF.
agent_relevance: A biased monitoring signal produces biased control even with identical memory. Shows how a wrong meta-level signal propagates down.

source: Metcalfe and Finn (2008), as described in Finn (2008)
finding: When JOLs were manipulated independently of recall, study choices followed the JOL.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Secondhand summary only.
agent_relevance: Same as the Finn (2008) line: control reads the signal, not the truth.

source: Goldsmith, Koriat and Weinberg-Eliezer (2002) Strategic regulation of grain size in memory reporting
finding: Extends the monitoring-and-control model of Koriat and Goldsmith (1996) from the withhold-or-report decision to choosing how precise to be. People give coarse answers when the fine answer is doubtful.
numbers: Exp 1 (about 40 participants, F(1,39)): Phase 1 accuracy of fine answers later volunteered at fine grain .50 vs .21 for those later reported coarse; coarse answers .88 vs .67. Overall fine .32, coarse .75. Fine grain chosen 41% of the time. Exp 2 replicated the pattern (fine .28, coarse .65).
limits: General-knowledge questions, undergraduates, explicit payoffs; demand characteristics cannot be fully ruled out.
agent_relevance: The reporting step can trade accuracy for detail by monitoring its own confidence. A model for answer-coarse-or-abstain decisions, which G6 limits.

source: Koriat and Goldsmith (1996) Monitoring and control processes in the strategic regulation of memory accuracy, as summarised in later papers
finding: Free report (option to withhold) lifts output accuracy well above forced report, at a cost in quantity. The gain depends on an accuracy incentive and on monitoring effectiveness.
numbers: No numbers recorded; PDF could not be parsed.
limits: Secondhand through abstracts and later papers.
agent_relevance: Withholding helps only if the monitor separates right from wrong. Ties to G6: abstain only with a good signal.

source: Rechdan et al. (2017) Computer mediated social comparative feedback does not affect metacognitive regulation of memory reports
finding: A null extension: social feedback about a co-witness did not change confidence, accuracy or detail level in Experiment 2. In Experiment 1, both feedback groups gave more fine-grain details than controls, with no difference by valence.
numbers: Exp 1 N=87 (15 of 54 feedback participants failed the manipulation check, leaving 69). Exp 2 N=90 (73 analysed). Confidence in fine-grain answers correlated with volunteering them, r(82)=0.49. No condition effect on confidence, F(2,83)=0.57.
limits: Computer-mediated feedback only; suspicion and exclusions reduce power. A boundary condition, not a refutation.
agent_relevance: The monitoring-control link was stable under this social manipulation. Our agent faces no such pressure, but related to sycophancy limits (G5).

source: Mazzoni and Cornoldi (1993) labor-in-vain effect, from a search summary
finding: Items given more study time were not recalled better, which looks like failed control. The effect stayed across five experiments and vanished only when the experimenter paced study.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Search snippet only. A 2024 study (Li et al., 62 students; snippet only) reports labor-and-gain instead, so the result depends on method.
agent_relevance: Control by effort is not always rewarded. Do not assume more thinking on a hard item repairs it (G11, G12).

source: Undorf and Ackerman (2017) The puzzle of study time allocation for the most challenging items
finding: Study time versus JOL is an inverted U across the hardest items. Time limits (a diminishing criterion) explain it better than data-driven allocation.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Abstract snippet only.
agent_relevance: The hardest items get less effort, so a per-item stop rule is needed rather than a fixed rule.

source: Callaway et al. (2024) optimal metacognition for memory recall, as cited in Oh and Gobet (2025)
finding: A resource-rational model of metamemory: a meta-level decision process that picks when to stop retrieval by cost and benefit. Seen only as cited in MGV.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Secondhand; original not opened.
agent_relevance: A normative form of the control rule that could set our stop thresholds.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) confidence elicitation: scale and sampling
finding: Better models are better monitors, but the gain is partial. Sampling more responses improves failure prediction and then levels off.
numbers: GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna average ECE above 0.377 (poorly calibrated). GPT-4 has lower ECE but average AUROC only 62.7%. More sampled responses raised performance significantly, then converged.
limits: Black-box methods; five models; none beat the others on every task.
agent_relevance: Spend a few samples to build the agreement signal, then stop. More than a handful adds little.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) self-evaluation limits
finding: Models judge their own samples better when shown several of their own samples first (brainstorming alternatives), and verification improves faster than generation with size. The model may be overconfident on its own samples.
numbers: Figure 1: 52B self-evaluation on five sampling tasks separates correct from incorrect samples; the paper notes models cannot tell their own tokens from tokens given by a third party.
limits: Qualitative in text; figures not extracted; a possible confound is that P(IK) may track question difficulty rather than self-knowledge (the authors say so in a footnote).
agent_relevance: Show alternatives, not only the candidate, when asking a model to check. Still, G5 says no authorship cues.
